The Elderly and Smartphones: A Bridge or a Barrier?

In the digital age, smartphones have become indispensable tools for communication, information, and daily life. However, for many elderly people, these devices present both opportunities and challenges. While smartphones can greatly improve the quality of life for seniors, their use also raises concerns about accessibility and social exclusion.

On the positive side, smartphones enable the elderly to stay connected with family and friends through video calls, messaging apps, and social media. This is particularly valuable for those who live alone or far from their loved ones. Additionally, smartphones provide convenient access to health information, online shopping, and emergency services, which can enhance their independence and safety. For example, a simple tap on the screen can summon medical help or remind them to take medication.

Nevertheless, the elderly often face significant barriers when using smartphones. Small screens, complex interfaces, and unfamiliar terminology can be frustrating. Many seniors struggle with touchscreens, fear making mistakes, or worry about privacy and fraud. As a result, some give up entirely, which may deepen their sense of isolation in an increasingly digital world.

To address these issues, society should take responsibility. Smartphone manufacturers can design senior-friendly models with larger buttons, simpler menus, and voice control. Community centers and family members can offer patient training and encouragement. More importantly, we should respect the elderly's pace and choices rather than forcing technology upon them.

In conclusion, smartphones are neither inherently good nor bad for the elderly—it depends on how we design and introduce them. With thoughtful support, these devices can serve as a bridge to a more connected and fulfilling life, rather than a barrier that leaves seniors behind.

title: 失败是成功之母

Ladies and gentlemen, distinguished guests, and fellow seekers of success,

Good morning/afternoon/evening.

I stand before you today not to talk about the glory of victory, but to speak of something far more valuable, yet far less celebrated: failure.

There is an old proverb that says, “Failure is the mother of success.” We’ve all heard it. But have we truly understood it? Or do we secretly still fear failure, avoid it, and treat it as something shameful?

Let me ask you: What if I told you that every great success story you admire is built not on a foundation of perfect wins, but on a graveyard of failures? Thomas Edison failed thousands of times before inventing a working lightbulb. J.K. Rowling was rejected by twelve publishers. Michael Jordan missed over 9,000 shots in his career. Yet we call them successes. Why? Because they refused to let failure be the final word.

Failure is not the opposite of success. It is a stepping stone to success. It is the mother who teaches us what doesn’t work, so we can discover what does. Every failed attempt carries a lesson. Every mistake holds a seed of improvement. But here’s the catch: the lesson only comes if we are willing to look for it.

Too many people give up after one fall. They see failure as a verdict on their worth. But failure is not a verdict — it is feedback. It is the universe saying, “Not this way. Try another.” The only true failure is giving up.

So how do we turn failure into our teacher? First, we change our mindset. Stop asking, “Why did I fail?” and start asking, “What did I learn?” Second, we embrace humility. The person who never fails is the person who never tries anything new. Third, we persist. Success is not a straight line; it is a zigzag of attempts, setbacks, and breakthroughs.

Think of a child learning to walk. They fall dozens of times. Do we scold them? Do we say, “You’re a failure”? No. We cheer them on. We help them up. We celebrate each wobbly step. So why do we treat our own adult failures so harshly? We must become that encouraging parent to ourselves.

Let me leave you with this thought: You are not defined by how many times you fall, but by how many times you rise. Every failure is a brick. You can either throw it at yourself, or you can use it to build a staircase to your dreams.

So go ahead. Fail. Fail boldly. Fail forward. Because when you do, you are not walking away from success — you are walking toward it, hand in hand with its mother.

Thank you.

 The Foundation of Well-being: A Guide to Healthy Eating

In our fast-paced modern world, the drive for convenience often overshadows the fundamental need for proper nutrition. Healthy eating is frequently perceived as a restrictive or complicated chore, but in reality, it is a simple and powerful practice that forms the very foundation of our physical and mental well-being. It is not about strict limitations or depriving oneself, but about nourishing the body with the fuel it needs to thrive.

At its core, healthy eating is about balance and variety. A truly healthy diet is not built on a single "superfood" but on a colourful tapestry of different food groups. This includes a rich supply of fruits and vegetables, which provide essential vitamins, minerals, and fibre. It involves choosing whole grains like oats and brown rice for sustained energy, and lean proteins such as fish, beans, and poultry for muscle repair and growth. Healthy fats, found in avocados, nuts, and olive oil, are also crucial for brain function and hormone production. The key is to consume these in appropriate proportions, ensuring the body receives a complete spectrum of nutrients.

The benefits of adopting such a diet are profound and far-reaching. Physically, it is our strongest defence against chronic conditions like heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity. A well-nourished body enjoys a stronger immune system, higher energy levels, and more restful sleep. Yet, the impact extends beyond the physical. A growing body of research links a nutritious diet to improved mental health, including better mood, sharper focus, and a reduced risk of depression and anxiety.

Ultimately, healthy eating is an act of self-care. It is a commitment to providing our bodies with the respect and nourishment they deserve. By making mindful choices—favouring whole foods over processed ones and listening to our body's hunger cues—we can build a sustainable lifestyle that enhances our quality of life for years to come. It is a journey, not a destination, and every wholesome meal is a step toward a healthier, happier self.

The Little Fox and the Moon

Once upon a time, in a cozy forest nestled between soft rolling hills, there lived a little fox named Rusty. Rusty had fur the color of autumn leaves and eyes that sparkled like dew. Every night, before curling up in his warm den, Rusty would sit at the edge of the forest and gaze up at the moon.

"Goodnight, Moon," he would whisper. And the moon, round and bright, would smile down at him.

But one night, Rusty noticed something strange. The moon was not round anymore. It was thin and curved, like a silver smile.

"Moon!" cried Rusty. "What happened to you? Are you feeling well?"

The moon did not answer, but its light seemed to flicker softly, as if it were laughing.

Rusty ran to his friend Ollie the Owl. "Ollie! Ollie! The moon is shrinking! We must help it!"

Ollie blinked his big round eyes and hooted softly. "Little Rusty, the moon is not shrinking. It is just changing its shape. It does this every month. Sometimes it is round, sometimes it is a crescent, and sometimes it hides entirely."

"But why?" asked Rusty, tilting his head.

"Because," said Ollie wisely, "even the moon needs to rest. When it hides, it is sleeping. And when it returns, it is bright and full again, ready to watch over us."

Rusty thought about this. He thought about how he, too, felt tired sometimes and needed to curl up and sleep. He thought about how he always woke up feeling fresh and happy.

"So the moon is just... taking a nap?" Rusty asked.

"Exactly," said Ollie.

Rusty smiled. He trotted back to his favorite spot at the edge of the forest and looked up at the thin crescent moon.

"Goodnight, Moon," he whispered. "Sleep well. I will wait for you to be round and bright again."

And as Rusty curled up in his den, he felt warm and safe. He knew that even when the moon was hiding, it was still there, watching over him. And when it returned, it would shine just as brightly as before.

The forest grew quiet. The stars twinkled like tiny night-lights. And Rusty closed his eyes, dreaming of moonlit meadows and silver smiles.

Goodnight, little one. Sleep tight. 🌙🦊

A Practical Guide to *Pride and Prejudice*

Step 1: Know What You’re Getting Into
*Pride and Prejudice* is a novel by Jane Austen, first published in 1813. It is a social comedy, a romance, and a sharp critique of class, marriage, and manners in Regency-era England. Do not expect car chases or explosions. Do expect witty dialogue, emotional tension, and one of the most famous slow-burn romances in English literature.

Step 2: Learn the Core Cast
- Elizabeth Bennet – The protagonist. Intelligent, witty, independent, and too quick to judge.
- Mr. Darcy – Rich, proud, socially awkward, and secretly decent.
- Jane Bennet – Elizabeth’s kind, beautiful, and optimistic older sister.
- Mr. Bingley – Darcy’s friendly, easily influenced best friend.
- Mr. Collins – A pompous, foolish clergyman and cousin of the Bennets.
- Wickham – A charming, dishonest militia officer.
- Mrs. Bennet – Elizabeth’s mother. Obsessed with marrying off her daughters.
- Mr. Bennet – Elizabeth’s father. Sarcastic, detached, and fond of Elizabeth.
- Lady Catherine de Bourgh – Darcy’s arrogant, controlling aunt.
- Caroline Bingley – Bingley’s snobbish sister, who wants Darcy for herself.

Step 3: Understand the Central Conflict
The Bennet family has five daughters and no male heir. When Mr. Bennet dies, the estate will pass to Mr. Collins. Therefore, the Bennet sisters must marry well or face poverty. This pressure drives much of the plot.

Step 4: Follow the Plot in Order
1. The new neighbor – Mr. Bingley rents Netherfield Park and falls for Jane.
2. The insult – At a ball, Darcy refuses to dance with Elizabeth and says she is “tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me.”
3. The proposal from Collins – Mr. Collins proposes to Elizabeth. She refuses. He then proposes to her friend Charlotte Lucas, who accepts.
4. The Wickham story – Wickham claims Darcy cheated him out of an inheritance. Elizabeth believes him.
5. The first proposal – Darcy confesses his love to Elizabeth but insults her family. She rejects him and accuses him of ruining Jane and Bingley’s relationship and wronging Wickham.
6. The letter – Darcy writes a letter explaining the truth: he separated Bingley and Jane because he thought Jane was indifferent, and Wickham tried to elope with Darcy’s 15-year-old sister.
7. Pemberley – Elizabeth visits Darcy’s estate and sees him differently. She realizes she misjudged him.
8. The Lydia scandal – Lydia runs away with Wickham. Darcy secretly saves the family from ruin by paying Wickham to marry her.
9. The second proposal – Darcy proposes again. Elizabeth accepts.
10. The double wedding – Darcy and Elizabeth marry, as do Bingley and Jane.

Step 5: Track the Major Themes
- Pride – Darcy’s arrogance and Elizabeth’s prejudice.
- Prejudice – Elizabeth’s false judgment of Darcy and Wickham.
- Class and money – Marriage is a financial transaction.
- Marriage – Austen contrasts good marriages (Darcy and Elizabeth, Jane and Bingley) with bad ones (Collins and Charlotte, Wickham and Lydia).
- First impressions – They are often wrong.

Step 6: Pay Attention to the Opening Line
“It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.” This is ironic. It means the opposite: society assumes every rich man is a marriage target. This sets the tone for the whole novel.

Step 7: Read the Key Scenes Carefully
- The Meryton ball (Darcy’s insult)
- The Netherfield ball (dancing, tension, Collins’s awkwardness)
- Collins’s proposal (comedy)
- Darcy’s first proposal (drama and rejection)
- Darcy’s letter (turning point)
- Pemberley visit (romantic awakening)
- Lady Catherine’s confrontation (Elizabeth stands her ground)
- Darcy’s second proposal (resolution)

Step 8: Understand the Social Rules
- Women could not easily earn money. Marriage was survival.
- A woman’s reputation was fragile. Lydia’s elopement could ruin all her sisters.
- Dancing was a form of courtship and social evaluation.
- Wealth, land, and connections mattered more than love in many marriages.
- A gentleman could not propose to a woman unless he had enough money.

Step 9: Study the Characters’ Arcs
- Elizabeth – From prejudiced and playful to self-aware and mature.
- Darcy – From proud and reserved to humble and open.
- Jane – From passive and trusting to still kind, but more aware.
- Mr. Bennet – From detached and ironic to regretful and responsible.
- Mrs. Bennet – Mostly static, but her fears are understandable.
- Lydia – From foolish and reckless to married but still foolish.
- Wickham – From charming victim to exposed villain.

Step 10: Know the Ending’s Meaning
The ending is not just a happy marriage. It is a moral resolution. Darcy and Elizabeth both change. Pride is humbled. Prejudice is corrected. Love wins, but only after self-knowledge.

Step 11: Use It in Conversation
If someone asks, “What is *Pride and Prejudice* about?” say: “It’s about a proud rich man and a prejudiced smart woman who misunderstand each other, grow, and fall in love. It’s also about how marriage was a business for women in the 1800s.”

Step 12: Watch or Read the Best Adaptations
- Read the novel first.
- Watch the 1995 BBC miniseries (faithful and detailed).
- Watch the 2005 film (romantic and visually beautiful).
- Avoid adaptations that turn it into pure romance without the social satire.

Step 13: Remember the Final Lesson
Do not judge too quickly. Do not let pride or prejudice make your decisions. Listen, reflect, and be willing to change your mind. That is the practical wisdom of *Pride and Prejudice*.

The Little Sandman’s Sleepy Secret

Once upon a time, in a soft little village tucked behind the clouds, there lived a kind old sandman named Papa Lull. Every night, he carried a bag of sleepy dust and climbed down a silver ladder to help children fall asleep.

But one evening, Papa Lull noticed a little girl named Mia sitting up in bed, wide awake.

“I can’t sleep,” Mia said. “My thoughts are too loud.”

Papa Lull smiled gently. “Then let me tell you a secret. Sleep comes best when we make friends with the night.”

He opened his bag, but instead of sprinkling dust right away, he whispered, “First, let’s make your bed a little nest.”

Mia tugged her blanket up to her chin. Papa Lull said, “Now close your eyes and breathe slowly, like a sleepy turtle.”

Mia breathed in... and out... in... and out.

“Next,” said Papa Lull, “think of your favorite quiet place.”

Mia imagined a warm meadow with soft grass and a sky full of stars.

“Now,” Papa Lull said, “let your toes go to sleep. Then your feet. Then your legs. Then your tummy. Then your hands. Then your arms. Then your shoulders. Then your face.”

Mia giggled. “My nose is sleepy!”

“Good,” said Papa Lull. “Your nose may sleep first.”

He sprinkled a tiny bit of sleepy dust, not too much, just enough to feel like a gentle breeze.

“And remember,” he said softly, “if you wake up in the night, you don’t have to worry. The moon is still there. The stars are still there. And I will come again tomorrow.”

Mia yawned. “Papa Lull?”

“Yes, little one?”

“Can you tell me one more thing?”

“Of course.”

“What do dreams taste like?”

Papa Lull thought for a moment. “Like warm milk with honey… and a little bit of moonlight.”

Mia smiled. Her eyes grew heavy. Her body felt soft and warm. The room was quiet. The night was kind.

And just before she fell asleep, she heard Papa Lull whisper, “Sleep well, sweet child. Tomorrow will be bright.”

Then Mia drifted into a dream where she floated on a cloud, and the stars sang her a lullaby.

And if you listen very carefully tonight, you might hear Papa Lull climbing down his silver ladder, coming to help you sleep, too.

The end.

title: 活着
text:
A Practical Guide to Living: Step by Step

 Step 1: Take Care of Your Body First
- Sleep 7–8 hours a night. Everything else falls apart without this.
- Eat real food most of the time. You don't need perfection — just consistency.
- Move your body daily, even if it's just a 20-minute walk.
- Drink water before you reach for caffeine or sugar.
- Go outside. Sunlight regulates your mood and sleep more than you think.

 Step 2: Manage Your Mind
- Notice your thoughts without believing all of them.
- Write things down when your head feels crowded. Paper is cheaper than therapy (though therapy helps too).
- Limit doomscrolling. You are what you consume.
- Practice saying "I don't know yet" instead of panicking about the future.
- Accept that some days will feel pointless. That's normal, not a sign you're failing.

 Step 3: Build a Few Real Relationships
- Choose depth over quantity. Two or three honest friends beat a hundred acquaintances.
- Reach out first. Most people are waiting for someone else to do it.
- Listen more than you speak. Ask follow-up questions.
- Set boundaries. Saying "no" protects your "yes."
- Let go of relationships that consistently drain you. Loyalty to the wrong people is not a virtue.

 Step 4: Handle Money Without Lying to Yourself
- Spend less than you earn. This one rule prevents most financial disasters.
- Build an emergency fund, even if it starts at $10 a week.
- Avoid debt for things that lose value.
- Learn one skill that pays more than your current one.
- Track your spending for one month. You'll be surprised where it goes.

 Step 5: Do Work That Means Something (to You)
- Not every job is a calling. Sometimes it's just funding your life — that's fine.
- But always be building something: a skill, a project, a portfolio.
- Show up consistently. Talent is overrated; reliability is rare.
- Ask for what you want. Rejection costs nothing but silence costs everything.
- Quit when staying costs more than leaving.

 Step 6: Make Peace With Time
- You will not do everything. Choose what matters and let the rest go.
- Stop waiting for the "right moment." It doesn't exist.
- Do hard things early in the day.
- Schedule rest like it's an appointment. Burnout is not a badge of honor.
- Remember: you're going to die. Not to be morbid — to be free.

 Step 7: When Things Go Wrong (They Will)
- Pause before reacting. Most bad decisions are made in the first 10 seconds.
- Ask: "Will this matter in 5 years?" If not, let it go.
- Ask for help. It's not weakness; it's efficiency.
- Grieve properly. Don't skip the sadness — it comes back bigger.
- Start again. And again. That's the whole game.

 Step 8: The Only Rule That Matters
- Keep going, but not blindly. Adjust, learn, forgive yourself, and take the next small step.

---

Final note: There is no perfect way to live. There is only *your* way — built one honest day at a time. Start with Step 1. Right now.

title: 诚信
text:
On Integrity: The Foundation of Trust and Character

Integrity, known in Chinese as 诚信 (chéngxìn), is one of the most enduring virtues in human civilization. It combines honesty (诚) with trustworthiness (信), forming a moral foundation upon which individuals, relationships, and societies are built. While the term originates in Chinese philosophy, its meaning resonates across cultures and eras, reminding us that a person's word should be as solid as stone.

The importance of integrity begins with the individual. A person of integrity speaks truthfully, keeps promises, and acts consistently with stated values, even when no one is watching. Confucius emphasized that without trustworthiness, a person has no standing in society: "If a man does not keep his word, I do not know what he can accomplish." Integrity is not merely about avoiding lies; it is about aligning one's actions with one's principles, especially when doing so is inconvenient or costly.

Integrity also serves as the glue of human relationships. Trust cannot be demanded—it must be earned through consistent honesty. Friendships deepen when words prove reliable; businesses thrive when contracts are honored; families remain strong when members feel safe telling one another the truth. When integrity erodes, suspicion fills the void, and cooperation becomes nearly impossible.

At the societal level, integrity is the invisible infrastructure of civilization. Markets depend on it, courts rely on it, and democratic institutions collapse without it. A society where lying is normalized may function briefly, but it ultimately pays a heavy price in corruption, cynicism, and broken trust.

In an age of rapid information and easy deception, 诚信 remains a radical and necessary choice. Cultivating integrity requires daily effort: telling the truth kindly, admitting mistakes, and honoring commitments. It is a quiet virtue, rarely celebrated loudly, yet it shapes character more than any talent. Ultimately, integrity is not merely a value we practice—it is the mirror in which our true selves are reflected.

Here is a staged, actionable checklist in English about the little sparrows in winter.

A Staged Implementation Checklist: Helping Winter Sparrows

Stage 1: Preparation (Late Autumn – Early Winter)
- [ ] Identify the sparrow species in your area (e.g., house sparrow, tree sparrow) and note their winter habits.
- [ ] Choose a sheltered spot for a feeding station—away from prevailing winds and safe from cats.
- [ ] Purchase or build a sturdy bird feeder (platform, hopper, or hanging type).
- [ ] Stock up on appropriate food: millet, cracked corn, sunflower hearts, and unsalted peanuts.
- [ ] Acquire a shallow water dish and a birdbath heater if temperatures drop below freezing.
- [ ] Set up a brush pile or dense shrub nearby for quick escape cover.

Stage 2: Initial Setup (First Frost)
- [ ] Install the feeder at a height of 1.5–2 meters, or place it on a pole with a baffle.
- [ ] Clean the feeder with a 10% bleach solution and let it dry completely.
- [ ] Fill the feeder with a small amount of food to let sparrows discover it.
- [ ] Place the water dish in a sunny, wind-protected spot.
- [ ] Check daily for the first week and refill only when the food is nearly gone.

Stage 3: Daily Winter Routine (December – February)
- [ ] Refill the feeder at the same time each morning (sparrows learn routines).
- [ ] Remove any wet or moldy food immediately to prevent disease.
- [ ] Break ice in the water dish each morning and refill with lukewarm water.
- [ ] Scatter a small handful of millet on the ground on very cold days (below -10°C).
- [ ] Observe from a distance—avoid sudden movements near the feeding area.
- [ ] Record daily: number of sparrows, weather, and any unusual behavior.

Stage 4: Severe Weather Response (Storms, Ice, Extreme Cold)
- [ ] Increase food quantity by 50% before a predicted snowstorm.
- [ ] Clear snow from the feeder and surrounding ground after each snowfall.
- [ ] Provide extra high-energy food: suet balls or peanut butter (unsalted, no xylitol).
- [ ] Check water sources every few hours—dehydration is a major winter risk.
- [ ] Create a temporary windbreak using plywood or a tarp if winds exceed 40 km/h.

Stage 5: Health and Safety Monitoring (Ongoing)
- [ ] Disinfect the feeder every two weeks with hot soapy water or a bleach solution.
- [ ] Remove droppings from perches and trays daily.
- [ ] Watch for sick birds (fluffed feathers, lethargy, labored breathing) and stop feeding for 1–2 weeks if disease appears.
- [ ] Keep cats indoors or install a bell on their collar.
- [ ] Avoid using pesticides or rodenticides near the feeding area.

Stage 6: Late Winter – Early Spring Transition (Late February – March)
- [ ] Gradually reduce food quantity as natural seeds and insects return.
- [ ] Clean the feeder thoroughly and store it if you plan to stop feeding.
- [ ] Leave the brush pile intact for nesting season.
- [ ] Note any changes in sparrow behavior (courtship, territorial calls).
- [ ] Replace water dish with a fresh one and continue providing water if dry spells occur.

Stage 7: Review and Next-Year Planning (April)
- [ ] Review your daily records: which foods were most consumed? Which days had the most visitors?
- [ ] Repair or replace any damaged feeder parts.
- [ ] Replenish food stocks for next winter during spring sales.
- [ ] Consider adding a second feeder to reduce crowding.
- [ ] Share your observations with a local birding group or citizen science project.

Key Reminders:
- Never feed bread, milk, or salted snacks.
- Keep feeders at least 2 meters from windows to prevent collisions.
- Wash hands after handling feeders or dead birds.

title: 海底两万里
text:
Good morning/afternoon, everyone.

It is a great honor to stand here today and share with you one of the most extraordinary adventure stories ever written — *Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea* by the visionary French author Jules Verne.

Imagine this: the year is 1866. Reports of a mysterious sea monster are terrorizing sailors across the world's oceans. Ships are disappearing. Panic is spreading. Three men — Professor Pierre Aronnax, his loyal servant Conseil, and the fearless harpooner Ned Land — set out to hunt this creature. But what they discover is far more astonishing than any monster: it is the *Nautilus*, a magnificent submarine commanded by the enigmatic and brilliant Captain Nemo.

From that moment on, we are plunged into a breathtaking journey beneath the waves. We glide through coral forests, walk on the ocean floor in diving suits, visit the lost city of Atlantis, battle giant squids, and witness the wonders of the deep — all through the eyes of Professor Aronnax.

But *Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea* is far more than a simple adventure tale. It is a profound exploration of some of the deepest questions of human existence.

First, it is a story about the pursuit of knowledge. Professor Aronnax represents the insatiable human curiosity to understand the world. He is willing to risk his life to study the ocean's secrets. Through him, Verne celebrates science, discovery, and the boundless power of the human mind.

Second, it is a story about freedom and captivity. Captain Nemo has built the *Nautilus* to escape the world of men. He has fled from tyranny, injustice, and the cruelty of nations. Yet in his quest for freedom, he has become a prisoner of his own hatred and isolation. The submarine is both his sanctuary and his cage. This raises a powerful question: can true freedom exist without connection to others?

Third, it is a story about the relationship between man and nature. The ocean in Verne's novel is not merely a setting — it is a living, breathing world of infinite beauty and terrifying power. Verne reminds us that nature is both a treasure to be admired and a force to be respected.

And finally, it is a story about the future. When Jules Verne wrote this novel in 1870, submarines barely existed. The idea of traveling twenty thousand leagues under the sea was pure fantasy. Yet Verne's imagination was so vivid, so scientifically grounded, that he predicted technologies that would not become reality for decades. He showed us that imagination is the first step toward invention.

Today, as we face challenges like climate change, ocean pollution, and the exploration of our own planet's final frontiers, the lessons of *Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea* feel more relevant than ever. The ocean covers more than seventy percent of our planet, yet we have explored less than five percent of it. The mysteries that Captain Nemo once guarded are still waiting to be discovered.

So I leave you with this thought: like Professor Aronnax, may we never stop being curious. Like the *Nautilus*, may we always push forward into the unknown. And like the vast ocean itself, may our imagination be deep, boundless, and full of wonder.

Thank you.

title: 家乡的春节
text:
Here's a bedtime fairy tale about the Spring Festival in a little hometown, written in English for you to read to your child.

---

The Little Lantern Who Wanted to Fly

In a cozy little town called Sweetwater, where the houses leaned close together like old friends, there lived a very small red lantern named Ling. Ling was the youngest lantern in Grandpa Chen's shop, and she had a secret wish.

"I want to fly," she whispered to the other lanterns. "Not just hang here. I want to touch the stars."

The older lanterns chuckled. "Lanterns don't fly, little one. We glow. That is enough."

But Ling didn't think glowing was enough. Every night, she watched the paper kites dance in the sky and dreamed.

Then one evening, just before the Spring Festival, a little girl named Mei came into the shop. She had lost her mother that year, and her eyes were sad.

"Grandpa Chen," Mei said softly, "I want a lantern to send a wish to Mama. But it has to be a special lantern. One that can fly."

Grandpa Chen looked at all his lanterns. They were beautiful, but none of them could fly.

Then Ling spoke—though only the wind heard her—"I can try."

And something magical happened. Ling's flame flickered brighter, and suddenly she felt lighter than air.

Grandpa Chen blinked. "Well," he said, "I've never seen a lantern do that before." He gently handed Ling to Mei. "Take her to the river, little one. The river knows the way to the sky."

Mei carried Ling to the riverbank, where the whole town had gathered for the Spring Festival. Firecrackers popped like tiny stars. Dumplings steamed in bamboo baskets. Grandmas told stories of dragons and lucky coins.

Mei knelt by the water. "Mama," she whispered, "I miss you. Happy New Year."

She placed Ling on the river. The little lantern floated, then rose—higher and higher, past the paper kites, past the moon, until she was just a tiny red dot among the stars.

And for a moment, Ling touched a star. It was warm, like a mother's hug.

From that night on, every Spring Festival in Sweetwater, children would write wishes on paper lanterns and send them down the river. And if you look very carefully, you might see one small red lantern that flies higher than all the rest—carrying a wish for someone who is loved.

The End.

---

Goodnight, little one. May your dreams fly as high as Ling's lantern.

title: 友谊的价值
text:
The Value of Friendship

Lily was a quiet girl who had just moved to a new city. She knew nobody at her new school, and every day felt long and lonely. She would sit by herself during lunch, watching other students laugh and chat in groups. She wished she could have a friend, but she was too shy to start a conversation.

One afternoon, during art class, the teacher asked everyone to pair up for a project. Lily's heart sank. She looked around nervously, hoping someone would choose her. Just then, a girl with bright eyes and a warm smile walked over. "Hi, I'm Mia. Want to be partners?" she asked. Lily nodded, relieved and grateful.

As they worked on the project together, they discovered they shared many interests—both loved drawing, reading mystery novels, and listening to the same music. They talked and laughed, and for the first time since moving, Lily felt happy. From that day on, Mia and Lily became inseparable. They ate lunch together, walked home together, and helped each other with homework.

One rainy day, Lily received terrible news: her grandmother, whom she loved dearly, had passed away. She was heartbroken. At school, she could barely hold back her tears. Mia noticed immediately and quietly sat beside her. She didn't say much—she just held Lily's hand and stayed with her. After school, Mia walked Lily home, carrying her umbrella and sharing it, even though it meant getting wet herself.

That evening, Mia showed up at Lily's door with a small handmade card and a box of cookies. "I'm here for you," she said simply. Lily burst into tears and hugged her tightly. In that moment, Lily understood what friendship truly meant. It wasn't just about having fun together—it was about being there when it mattered most.

Weeks passed, and with Mia's support, Lily began to heal. She realized that friendship is one of the most valuable things in life. It gives us strength when we are weak, comfort when we are sad, and joy when we are happy. A true friend is like a lighthouse in the storm—steady, bright, and always guiding you home.

Lily never forgot that rainy day, and she never forgot Mia's kindness. She learned that friendship is not measured by how long you've known someone, but by how deeply you care. And she promised herself that she would always be that kind of friend to others—someone who shows up, who stays, and who loves without condition.

Because in the end, the value of friendship is priceless.
